The ending without applause

Our drama group usually ended performances with a loud song. For a new play about a lost friendship, the director suggested something ____1____: the actors would leave one by one, and the final character would close a book in silence. I thought the audience would not know when to ____2____. Without a bright ending, I feared our work might seem ____3____.

At rehearsal, we tried both versions. The song gave an immediate burst of energy, but its cheerful mood seemed to ____4____ the scene before it. The silent version left the final words in the room. Our director did not tell us which to prefer. She asked what each ending invited the audience to ____5____. We began discussing purpose rather than simply choosing the most ____6____ sound.

We invited another class to watch the alternatives. Their responses were mixed. Some wanted the song; others said the quiet ending stayed with them longer. One pupil suggested a short lighting change to make the finish ____7____. A member of staff tried it while we repeated the last scene. The signal solved my practical concern without changing the ending's ____8____. Silence no longer had to mean ____9____.

On performance day, the room remained quiet for a moment after the book closed. I felt the old urge to fill the pause. Then applause began. It was not necessarily better than the response to a cheerful song; it belonged to a different ____10____. Afterwards, a teacher mentioned a line from the play rather than its ending trick. That pleased our writer, who wanted the story to remain ____11____. The final silence had supported the work instead of becoming a separate ____12____.

We did not automatically repeat it next time. A comedy might need another rhythm. I had learned that an ending should answer the piece's needs, not merely follow our group's ____13____. The quiet moment had been a choice we could explain, not a rule for every show. I still enjoyed a loud finale. I simply had more than one way to recognise a performance reaching its ____14____, and more patience with the moment before the audience ____15____.

Their arrangement allows sections to move into position without requiring the whole sheet to pass through ____4____. Following the wrong direction can make the paper resist. More force may produce damage rather than a useful ____5____. A careful user looks for the existing pattern before trying to ____6____ it.

In a fictional project, students found no instance of a regional word in recorded interviews. One concluded that nobody used it anymore. The teacher asked whether the collection could ____1____ such a broad claim. It contained only a small number of speakers, mostly discussing work. A word associated with family meals might simply have had little ____2____ to occur. The empty search was a result within a sample, not a complete ____3____ of the language.

The group examined how the collection had been assembled. Participants came from several towns, but not every age group was equally ____4____. Unequal recording lengths also meant speakers contributed different amounts. The teacher asked them to describe these limits before treating the sample as ____5____. Its value did not require representing everyone. A clearly described limited collection could still answer a more ____6____ question.

The students revised their report to say that the word had not been found in the selected interviews. They then asked what further evidence would help. A targeted conversation about meals might offer a relevant setting, but prompting someone with the word itself would change the kind of evidence ____7____. Recognition after a prompt was not the same as spontaneous use. The distinction mattered because the proposed conclusion concerned ordinary speech ____8____. The method needed to match the ____9____.

Later, an older participant used the word in a separate interview. This did not prove that it was common throughout the region. It did, however, contradict the claim that ____10____ used it. The first sample had not been worthless; the original interpretation had been too ____11____. They recorded the new instance without another universal claim. Evidence could change the account without becoming an excuse to ____12____ between extremes.

The final presentation showed the searches, sample boundaries and later example. Its conclusion was modest but more informative. The students had learned to distinguish a measured absence from an assertion of nonexistence. Speech could not be reduced to one search box. A good collection was a resource for ____13____, not an authority that settled every possible question. The missing word had made them examine the ____14____ around their result. The later example then gave them something specific to ____15____.
